parts.partTitle: The Owning Side & Silent NULL Foreign Keys

beats.headline: Why is your database foreign key saving as NULL?
beats.subline: Updating only the Java list does nothing to the underlying database foreign key.
beats.narration: In Java, object references look symmetrical. In SQL, only one table holds the foreign key. Mutate only the inverse list, and Hibernate quietly writes NULL straight into your database foreign key column.

beats.title: Java Object Graph vs SQL Foreign Key

top.label: Inverse Side Only
points: Hibernate completely ignores inverse collection writes
Foreign key author_id written as NULL in database

bottom.label: Owning Side Updated
points: Physical foreign key owner reference set
Clean INSERT statement with valid foreign key ID

beats.narration: Hibernate checks only the owning side when writing foreign keys. Calling author dot getBooks dot add book leaves book dot author null, so Hibernate writes NULL to the author id foreign key.

beats.title: Encapsulating Synchronized Helper Methods

steps.explanation: Declares inverse side; Book entity field manages physical foreign key column.
Keeps both Java list and owning reference synced in a single call.

beats.narration: Fix this with synchronized helper methods on the parent entity. Inside addBook, add the item to the internal collection and call book dot setAuthor passing this, keeping both sides perfectly in sync.

beats.title: Hibernate SQL Generation Check
beats.caption: Comparing raw collection mutation against helper method

lines.text: # 1. Mutating inverse list directly without book.setAuthor(author):
INSERT INTO books (id, title, author_id) VALUES (101, '1984', NULL);
INSERT INTO books (id, title, author_id) VALUES (101, '1984', 1);

beats.narration: Check the SQL output. Mutating the list alone produces an insert statement with a null author id. Using the helper method sets the foreign key cleanly on the initial insert statement.

beats.title: Owning Side Rules Locked In
takeaways: Owning side controls foreign key SQL writes
mappedBy marks inverse side for queries & traversal
Encapsulate collection changes with helper methods
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Unidirectional SQL traps & lazy @OneToOne with @MapsId →
beats.narration: That is the owning side rule. Up next in Part 2, see why unidirectional OneToMany fires extra update statements and how MapsId rescues lazy loading on OneToOne.

beats.headline: Unidirectional @OneToMany executes extra UPDATE statements.
beats.subline: Omitting @ManyToOne on child entities degrades database write performance.
beats.narration: Unidirectional OneToMany looks clean in code, but behind the scenes Hibernate executes extra SQL updates for every single child row. Here is why skipping ManyToOne destroys your query efficiency.

beats.title: Unidirectional @OneToMany Execution Overhead
beats.subtitle: Why inserting 2 items requires 4 database queries

nodes.label: INSERT Order
nodes.detail: Parent row persisted with generated ID 1

nodes.label: INSERT Child Items
nodes.detail: Child rows persisted with NULL order_id column

nodes.label: UPDATE Foreign Keys
nodes.detail: Extra UPDATE statements executed per child row to set order_id

beats.narration: When the child entity has no parent reference, Hibernate inserts child rows with a null foreign key first. Then it fires a second update statement per child row to attach the parent ID.

beats.title: Preserving Lazy Loading with @MapsId

steps.explanation: UserProfile shares the exact primary key value of User.id.
Maps primary key directly to foreign key, keeping lazy fetch intact.

beats.narration: For OneToOne, bidirectional mapping breaks lazy loading because Hibernate checks if the target exists. Using MapsId on the child shares the parent primary key, eliminating inverse fields while guaranteeing lazy loading.

beats.title: Bidirectional @OneToOne vs @MapsId

top.label: Bidirectional Foreign Key
points: Fires immediate SELECT to check non-null target
Requires separate foreign key column & unique index

bottom.label: @MapsId Shared Primary Key
points: Zero extra queries when loading parent entity

beats.narration: Standard bidirectional OneToOne executes an immediate select query to check nullability even with lazy fetch. Using MapsId reuses the parent primary key, eliminating that extra select query completely.

beats.title: Mapping Optimization Complete
takeaways: Explicitly override default EAGER fetch to LAZY
Use @MapsId on @OneToOne for safe lazy loading
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The @ManyToMany List penalty & explicit join entities →
beats.narration: Now you understand table mappings. In Part 3, discover why using List on ManyToMany triggers a full table wipe and how explicit join entities save performance.

beats.headline: Using List on @ManyToMany wipes out entire join tables.
beats.subline: Removing one element forces Hibernate to execute full table deletes and re-inserts.
beats.narration: Removing a single tag from a ManyToMany List causes Hibernate to wipe out every single join row for that post and re-insert them all. Let's fix that bag penalty.

beats.title: List vs Set SQL Deletion Penalty
beats.caption: Removing 1 tag from a post with 5 tags

lines.text: # Using List<Tag>: Hibernate deletes ALL join rows and re-inserts
# Using Set<Tag>: Single targeted DELETE statement executed
DELETE FROM post_tags WHERE post_id = 10 AND tag_id = 5;

beats.narration: Look at the generated SQL. With List, Hibernate executes a total delete of all post tags followed by re-inserts. Switching to Set lets Hibernate issue one targeted delete for that single row.

beats.title: Promoting Join Table to First-Class Entity

steps.explanation: Composite primary key containing studentId and courseId fields.
Promotes join table to entity supporting grade & enrollment date.

beats.narration: When join tables store attributes like grade or date, promote ManyToMany to an explicit join entity. Connect it using EmbeddedId for the composite primary key and MapsId on two ManyToOne fields.

beats.title: Explicit Join Entity Architecture
beats.subtitle: Adding custom fields to join tables safely

nodes.label: Enrollment Entity
nodes.detail: Join entity with grade, date & composite PK

beats.narration: Instead of hidden join tables, explicit join entities convert multi-table links into clean domain objects with full auditing attributes, backed by precise foreign key constraints.

beats.title: Join Table Best Practices
takeaways: Always map @ManyToMany with Set, never List
Promote join tables with extra fields to entities

parts.partTitle: Cascades, Orphan Removal & Preventing Data Loss

beats.headline: CascadeType.REMOVE on @ManyToOne can destroy your database.
beats.subline: Deleting one user record can delete shared system application roles.
beats.narration: Putting CascadeType REMOVE on a ManyToOne association can quietly wipe out shared application roles across your entire database. Here is how to configure cascades safely without risking data loss.

beats.title: CascadeType.REMOVE vs orphanRemoval

top.label: CascadeType.REMOVE
points: Deletes child rows ONLY when parent entity is deleted
Removing item from list leaves orphan in database

bottom.label: orphanRemoval = true
points: Deletes child row when removed from Java collection
Also deletes child rows when parent is deleted

beats.narration: Cascade REMOVE deletes child records only when the parent entity itself is removed. Orphan removal goes further, deleting child rows whenever you remove them from the parent collection.

beats.title: Safe Aggregate Root Cascading

steps.explanation: Propagates lifecycle actions down to exclusively owned children.
Cleans up orphaned records when removed from items list.

beats.narration: Combine CascadeType ALL and orphanRemoval only on true parent-child aggregates like Order and OrderItem. Never put REMOVE cascades on shared lookup entities like User roles or system tags.

beats.title: Entity Relationship Rules Checklist
beats.caption: Rules for safe entity relationship mapping

lines.text: # Rule 1: Always set fetch = LAZY on @ManyToOne & @OneToOne
# Rule 2: Cascade downwards inside aggregate boundaries only
# Rule 3: NEVER cascade REMOVE upward or across shared entities

beats.narration: Follow three golden rules: set fetch to LAZY on all ManyToOne and OneToOne fields, cascade downward strictly inside aggregate roots, and never cascade REMOVE to shared entities.

beats.title: Master Entity Relationships
takeaways: Cascade ONLY down owned parent-child aggregates
Never put CascadeType.REMOVE on shared lookups
